item.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Introduces Workload Recovery and Infrastructure Checks
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Introduces Workload Recovery and Infrastructure Checks

Today, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod introduces workload recovery and infrastructure checks. These features catch failures sooner and raise the goodput of training workloads.

🧩 The Challenge

Large training jobs can fail even when every node looks healthy. A GPU with a subtle fault can pass its stress tests and still return wrong values. When a job stalls on an NCCL timeout, it keeps its GPUs, and Slurm still shows it as running. If a device plugin crashes on one node, the job fails with an error that never mentions the plugin.

Teams usually find these problems only after the loss diverges or the job fails, and by then, the compute is spent. Each of these failures lowers goodput, the share of your cluster’s time that goes to useful training.

Types of Failures

  • Numerical faults: A GPU can pass every hardware test and still compute wrong results. The first sign is often NaN or infinite loss in a production run.
  • Hung jobs: An NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock can stop a job without ending it. The job keeps its GPUs and their memory, and Slurm reports it as running until someone checks the loss curve or the log.
  • Cluster-level failures: Some failures happen in Kubernetes, not in a node’s hardware. A device plugin crash-loops, a required DaemonSet never starts on a new node, or ranks on different nodes fall out of step in an NCCL collective. When the job fails, the error often doesn’t say which pod or node caused it.

🛡️ New Infrastructure Checks

The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors, deep health checks test nodes during provisioning, and automatic node recovery reboots or replaces faulty hardware.

Monitoring Agents and Checks

Feature Description
Health Monitoring Agent (HMA) Watches each node for GPU errors such as Xid and NVLink faults, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) errors, and kernel errors.
MultiNodeTrainingValidation A new deep health check for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). When HyperPod provisions an instance, or when you run the check on demand, it trains a small model on the instance and then across instances of the same type. The instance fails if the loss becomes NaN or infinite, or training doesn’t finish in time.
Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent Watches the Kubernetes layer of an EKS cluster for problems such as crash-looping device plugins, missing DaemonSets, and tainted nodes. When a job fails, it reports the pods and nodes involved as Kubernetes events and Amazon CloudWatch logs.
Hung Job Detection Finds Slurm jobs that have stopped making progress. An agent on each node watches the job’s output and GPU activity, or log patterns that you define. It writes an event to CloudWatch and can cancel the job so that Slurm requeues it.

⚙️ Existing Resiliency Features

The existing HyperPod resiliency features check a single node at a time.

  • InstanceStress: Runs DCGM level 4 diagnostics and tests each instance’s GPUs, GPU memory, NVLink, and EFA devices.
  • InstanceConnectivity: Runs NCCL tests across GPU instances, or NCCOM tests on AWS Trainium.

🚀 Availability

These checks run when instances are provisioned, or on demand, and confirm that their GPUs train correctly. Hung job detection runs alongside each Slurm job and catches a job that has stopped making progress.

#SageMakerHyperPod #MachineLearning #GPUComputing #Kubernetes #AWSInfrastructure

Source: Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod | Amazon Web Services

item.title: NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning Enables Shared GPU Memory on EKS
item.description:
NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning Enables Shared GPU Memory on EKS

NVIDIA has open-sourced Run:ai, an AI workload orchestration platform for Kubernetes, and validated a GPU Fractioning capability that allows multiple Pods to share a single GPU on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). In the validated example, two Pods successfully shared one NVIDIA A10G Tensor Core GPU on an EC2 g5.xlarge instance, each allocating 6 GiB within an 8 GiB memory limit while an allocation above the limit was rejected as expected.

🔍 Overview

GPU sharing is not new — Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), time-slicing, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) address different isolation and utilization needs. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning builds on MPS with Kubernetes-integrated scheduling, per-Pod memory contracts, enforcement, and metrics. The GPU Fractioning Operator helps several teams share one or two GPUs, addressing scenarios where notebooks, model evaluations, and small inference services leave teams waiting even when GPU memory remains available.

🧩 How it works

In the baseline configuration, the NVIDIA device plugin exposes a single GPU as one nvidia.com/gpu resource with GPU sharing disabled. Two Pods each requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 cannot run concurrently on that node, even when their combined GPU-memory demand fits. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds:

  • Kubernetes scheduling integration via the KAI Scheduler
  • Enforced GPU-memory limits per Pod
  • Per-Pod GPU-memory metrics

The approach applies to NVIDIA GPUs that meet the GPU Fractioning Operator’s hardware and software requirements, including GPUs without MIG. It uses NvFractions annotations, not Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA).

⚙️ Key details

Component Detail
Validated GPU NVIDIA A10G Tensor Core GPU (23,028 MiB)
Validated instance Amazon EC2 g5.xlarge
System node m7i.large hosting operator controllers and KAI Scheduler
GPU worker OS Custom Amazon Linux 2023 (AL2023)
GPU driver NVIDIA R615 driver branch
Container runtime containerd with NVIDIA Container Toolkit
Sharing mechanism MPS via fractiond with Node Resource Interface (NRI) integration
Metrics collection metricsd daemon exports per-Pod GPU-memory metrics
Compute modes Time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing
Error domains Separate workload error domains for default mode; shared error domain for sm-sharing (not security guarantees)

Each Pod receives an 8 GiB GPU-memory limit and allocates 6 GiB. The KAI Scheduler places both Pods on a tainted g5.xlarge node. The walkthrough establishes a whole-GPU baseline, verifies 6 GiB allocations, inspects per-Pod metrics, tests rejection of a 9 GiB allocation, and cleans up the disposable environment.

🚀 Availability

NVIDIA announced the open source release of NVIDIA Run:ai on October 13, 2026. This walkthrough uses two of its four modular components: KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator. KAI Resource Management and Workload Map address organizational governance and additional workload types, outside this walkthrough’s scope. Other configurations require compatibility checks and validation.

💡 Why it matters

Choose GPU fractioning when you need enforced per-Pod GPU-memory limits on GPUs without MIG and can run fixed-size GPU node groups. A memory limit does not reserve proportional compute. This walkthrough tests memory limits, not fault containment or compute performance. The solution enables better GPU utilization for workloads that don’t require a full GPU, reducing wait times for development and inference tasks.

#NVIDIA #Kubernetes #GPU #EKS #AI #Run:ai

Source: Using NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Flux v2 and GitOps Toolkit Launch for Kubernetes
item.description:
Flux v2 and GitOps Toolkit Launch for Kubernetes

Flux version 2 (v2) has been released, built from the ground up to use the Kubernetes API extension system. It integrates with the GitOps Toolkit, a set of composable APIs and specialized tools designed for building continuous delivery on top of Kubernetes.

🔍 Overview

Flux is an open and extensible continuous delivery solution for Kubernetes that keeps clusters in sync with sources of configuration, such as Git repositories and OCI artifacts. It automates updates to configuration when there is new code to deploy. The project is a Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) graduated project, used in production by various organizations and cloud providers.

🧩 How it works

The GitOps Toolkit consists of the APIs and controllers that make up the runtime for Flux v2. These APIs comprise Kubernetes custom resources, which can be created and updated by cluster users or other automation tooling. Flux v2 is constructed to integrate with Prometheus and other core components of the Kubernetes ecosystem.

⚙️ Key details

Version 2 introduces several long-requested features, including:

  • Support for multi-tenancy
  • Ability to sync an arbitrary number of Git repositories
  • Extensibility through the composable APIs of the GitOps Toolkit

Users can use the toolkit to extend Flux or to build custom systems for continuous delivery.

🚀 Availability

To get started, users can refer to the available guide on how to bootstrap Flux on Kubernetes and deploy a sample application in a GitOps manner. Developer guides are also available for those wishing to build their own systems using the toolkit.

#Kubernetes #GitOps #ContinuousDelivery #Flux #CNCF

Source: fluxcd/flux2

item.title: NVIDIA Upstreams Agent Substrate and Introduces Snapshot, NVKE, and NVKR
item.description:
NVIDIA Upstreams Agent Substrate and Introduces Snapshot, NVKE, and NVKR

NVIDIA is contributing upstream to Agent Substrate—an open-source agent runtime donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox—while introducing NVIDIA Snapshot, NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE), and NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR) as part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform.

🔍 Overview

Agent Substrate, NVIDIA Snapshot, NVKE, and NVKR address infrastructure needs across AI agent session management, GPU workload startup times, and managed Kubernetes cluster operations.

Component Description Status / License
Agent Substrate Security-hardened runtime that multiplexes sandboxed agent sessions over worker Pods Donated to CNCF Sandbox
NVIDIA Snapshot Checkpoint and restore system for GPU workloads on Kubernetes Open-source (DSX AI Factory)
NVKE Software to run managed Kubernetes clusters on factory infrastructure Apache 2.0 (Public Preview)
NVKR Reproducible builds for OS images, container images, and Helm charts Apache 2.0 (Public Preview)

🧩 How Agent Substrate Works

Agent Substrate provides a security-hardened, zero-trust runtime engineered to run agents and tools with 10x higher density than standard containers by decoupling actor state from worker Pods:

  • Session Multiplexing: Idle sessions are snapshotted out of gVisor or microVM sandboxes—including memory and filesystem state—freeing the underlying worker Pod.
  • Bypassing Control Plane Latency: Restoring an actor onto a free worker Pod skips API server, admission, etcd, scheduler, and kubelet roundtrips.
  • Kubernetes Integration: Worker Pods remain standard Kubernetes Pods, ensuring cluster scheduling, placement policies, and quotas continue to apply.
  • Upstream Capabilities: Public developments include router request parking (#221), request line protection for running actors (#1229), and Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) device pluggability (#752), with NVIDIA GPUs designated as the first supported device.

⚡ NVIDIA Snapshot GPU Checkpoint and Restore

NVIDIA Snapshot eliminates repeated workload initialization by saving fully initialized CPU and GPU memory states into portable artifacts:

  • Operations: Checkpointing is managed via PodSnapshot or SnapshotJob custom resources, while restoration uses the nvidia.com/restore-from Pod annotation.
  • Workload Compatibility: Features examples for vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM, and supports single-node multi-GPU workloads across tensor parallelism (TP), data and expert parallelism (DEP), and decode context parallelism (DCP).
  • Restoration Speed: Across tested configurations, Snapshot restores replicas in 3.6 to 42.7 seconds—8x to 36x faster than cold starts. Crusoe reduced GLM-5.3 Pod readiness from ~8 minutes to 31 seconds on NVIDIA HGX B300, while Saturn Cloud cut vLLM startup from 2–8.5 minutes to 6–34 seconds.

🛠️ NVKE and NVKR Infrastructure Tools

NVKE and NVKR allow AI factories to construct and operate managed Kubernetes services:

  • NVKR (NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes): Builds validated operating system images, container images, binaries, and Helm charts based on specific GPU generations and software versions.
  • NVKE (NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine): Deploys management and workload clusters using artifacts produced by NVKR, leveraging Cluster API infrastructure provider CAPNICo and NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo).
  • Node Identity & Observability: Requires nodes to present an attested SPIFFE identity before receiving join credentials, and exports telemetry via an OpenTelemetry-based Helm chart over OTLP.
  • Certification: NVKE is a Certified Kubernetes AI Platform and Certified Kubernetes Installer tested on Kubernetes 1.36.

#Kubernetes #NVIDIA #AIAgents #GPUInfrastructure #CloudNative

Source: Agent Substrate: Advancing Kubernetes for Agents at Scale | NVIDIA Technical Blog Source: Start and Restore GPU Workloads in Seconds with NVIDIA Snapshot | NVIDIA Technical Blog Source: Manage Kubernetes Clusters for GPU Infrastructure with NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform adds open‑source tools for reliable GPU‑Kubernetes clusters
item.description:
NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform adds open‑source tools for reliable GPU‑Kubernetes clusters

One underperforming GPU can slow an entire distributed training job, so measuring goodput – the volume of work successfully completed – is a more useful way to gauge cluster efficiency. NVIDIA’s DSX AI Factory Platform bundles the technologies needed to design, build, and operate efficient, resilient AI factories.

🔍 Overview

  • The platform’s open‑source software layer, NVIDIA DSX OS, provides tools for configuring, certifying, and maintaining the health of accelerated Kubernetes infrastructure.
  • It aims to keep every GPU, node, and network component in a ready state so that goodput remains high across large training jobs.

🛠️ Components

Component What it does
NVIDIA DSX OS Configures, certifies, and maintains accelerated Kubernetes clusters.
NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) Establishes a reproducible, version‑locked baseline for GPU‑optimized Kubernetes infrastructure; renders configuration recipes as bundles for existing deployment tools.
NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine (NVCRE) Validates cluster readiness for production workloads; tests GPUs, networking, and storage with AI workloads and diagnostics; records certification results and flags faulty nodes.
NVSentinel Monitors cluster health; publishes node conditions based on GPU, node, and network health; cordons or taints unhealthy nodes, drains workloads, remediates faults, and can trigger re‑validation with NVCRE before returning nodes to service.

All three projects are licensed under Apache 2.0 and welcome external contributions.

⚙️ How it works

  • AICR defines the cluster’s software baseline in version‑controlled files and renders them into artifacts that any deployment tool can apply.
  • Declarative templates detect configuration drift from manual changes and keep node configurations consistent after repairs.
  • Each recipe entry pins a component version, declares required healthy dependencies, and includes a healthCheckAsserts block that runs after installation.
  • The health assertions filter on the container waiting reason rather than the pod phase alone.
  • The bundle command produces ready‑to‑use artifacts: 
    1

    aicr bundle --recipe recipe.yaml --deployer argocd --output ./bundles
  • The --deployer flag accepts helm, argocd, argocd‑helm, flux, or helmfile, so the same validated recipe can become Argo CD Application manifests, Flux resources, a Helmfile release graph, or plain Helm commands.
  • Because the recipe is a file, standard version‑control workflows (history, code review, drift detection) manage the baseline.
  • Drift detection can be enforced as a CI gate: 
    1

    aicr diff --baseline ./golden.yaml --target cm://default/aicr-snapshot --fail-on-drift

📊 Measuring Efficiency

  • Goodput focuses on the actual work completed, highlighting the impact of any slow GPU on overall training performance.

🚀 Availability

  • The DSX OS, AICR, NVCRE, and NVSentinel projects are all open source under the Apache 2.0 license.
  • External contributions are encouraged, and the tools integrate with common GitOps deployment pipelines.

#NVIDIA #Kubernetes #AIInfrastructure #GPUClusters

Source: Configure, Certify, and Operate Kubernetes GPU Clusters with NVIDIA DSX OS | NVIDIA Technical Blog
